ap_psychology-m01.stem: A neuron fires only when the combined input it receives reaches its threshold of +15 units. It receives excitatory signals of +10 and +8 and an inhibitory signal of -5 at the same moment. Later, an additional excitatory signal of +4 arrives. Which statement best describes what happens?

options.text: It fires at first, because +10 and +8 together exceed the threshold, and it fires a larger action potential after the additional signal.
options.why: The inhibitory signal reduces the net input to +13, below threshold, and the size of an action potential does not depend on how far threshold is exceeded.

options.text: It does not fire at first, and it still does not fire after the additional signal, because inhibitory signals permanently block firing.
options.why: Inhibition lowers the net input only while it lasts; the net input becomes +17 and reaches threshold.

options.text: It does not fire at first, and it fires after the additional signal, with a smaller action potential because inhibition was present earlier.
options.why: An action potential is all-or-none; its size does not depend on earlier inhibition.

options.text: It does not fire at first, since the net input is +13, then fires after the added signal with a normal-size action potential.
options.why: The net input of +13 is below threshold, adding +4 brings it to +17, and an action potential is all-or-none in size once threshold is reached.

options.text: Signals travel faster along the affected axons, because the missing myelin lets the action potential spread more widely.
options.why: Myelin speeds conduction, so losing it slows signals rather than speeding them.

options.text: Neurotransmitters can no longer be released at the terminal buttons, because myelin is where they are manufactured and stored.
options.why: Neurotransmitters are stored in vesicles in the terminal buttons, not in the myelin sheath.

options.text: Dendrites cannot receive signals from other neurons, because the myelin sheath is the structure that receives incoming messages.
options.why: Dendrites and the cell body receive incoming messages, and the myelin sheath surrounds the axon.

options.text: Signals travel more slowly along the affected axons, because the myelin sheath normally speeds up conduction.
options.why: The myelin sheath insulates the axon and speeds the movement of the action potential, so damage to it slows or disrupts signaling.

options.why: Her movement is normal, so the motor cortex in the frontal lobe is not the damaged area.

options.why: Each hemisphere mainly processes touch from the opposite side of the body, so left parietal damage affects the right hand.
